feed.title: A Fragmented Peninsula
feed.subtitle: Additions to the collections – new entries, essays and maps – and the entries rewritten by hand.

entry.title: New entry: The passes
entry.summary: The escarpment is a wall with a few doors: the ghats, where a stream has cut the lava pile back far enough for a track. Everything that ever moved between the coast and the plateau – horses, armies, cotton, a railway – went through them, and the states that held them held the Deccan.
entry.content:
The Great Escarpment drops six hundred to a thousand metres from the plateau to the Konkan along its whole length, in steps of lava flow and scree, and for most of that length it cannot be climbed with a load. Where a west-flowing stream has bitten back into the wall, the flows step down more gently and a path can be made: these are the ghats – Thal above Kasara, Bhor above Khopoli, Nane above Junnar, Malshej, Varandha, Ambenali, Amba above Ratnagiri, Kumbharli above Chiplun, Phonda, Anmod above Goa – perhaps a dozen usable crossings in seven hundred kilometres. Each is a notch in the same rock, a few hundred metres wide, commanded by whatever stands above it.

They have been the plateau’s doors since there were goods to carry. Nane Ghat has a cave at its head cut in the first century BC by the Satavahanas, with an inscription of the queen Naganika and a great stone jar at the roadside for tolls: the earliest customs post in the peninsula, on the road from the port of Sopara to the capital at Paithan. The horse trade of the Deccan timeline came the same way, up from Chaul and Dabhol to Bijapur and Vijayanagara, and the sultanates’ Konkan revenue came down it. Shivaji’s state was, in one reading, a state of the passes: Rajmachi and Lohagad above the Bhor Ghat, Pratapgad above the Par and Ambenali ghats, Torna and Rajgad above the Velhe country, each fort set where it could close a door, and his Konkan campaigns were fought to hold both ends of them. The Company understood the same geography from below. Bombay’s value was that it lay under the two easiest crossings, Thal and Bhor; the road up the Bhor Ghat, opened in 1830, was among the first things the Company built in the conquered Deccan, and the railway incline that replaced it between 1856 and 1863 – tunnels and viaducts up a gradient of one in thirty-seven, with a reversing station at the top, built by a labour force that cholera and the cliff killed in thousands – put the plateau a day from the port and the cotton of the black soil on the Lancashire market.

The passes are still the seam. The expressway and the railway use Bhor, the pipelines and the pilgrims use Thal, and the older ghats are footpaths in the monsoon forest with a fort above each, the way they were when a fort was what a pass was for.

In the story

If the escarpment is the Deccan’s defining landform, the passes are where it was negotiated: the dozen places the rock allowed traffic, and therefore the dozen places a state could tax it, block it or pour an army through it. The Satavahana toll jar and the reversing station at Khandala are the same idea in different centuries.

entry.title: New entry: The rain shadow and the famines
entry.summary: The escarpment wrings the monsoon out over the Ghats and leaves the plateau behind it dry; the belt in its shadow is where the Deccan’s famines fell, and where the Company first learned to count the dead.
entry.content:
The Great Escarpment is a wall a thousand kilometres long facing the wind. The south-west monsoon arrives off the Arabian Sea loaded with water, climbs it, and drops most of what it carries on the crest: Mahabaleshwar takes six metres of rain in a season and Agumbe more; the Konkan below takes three. Fifty kilometres east the clouds have given up most of their load, and the plateau lives on the remainder – seven hundred millimetres at Pune, half that at Sholapur, Bijapur and Bellary, falling in a few months and varying from year to year by a third or more. This is the rain shadow, and it is the geography of the Deccan’s hunger: a belt running from Khandesh through the Bombay Deccan into the Ceded Districts and the Hyderabad country, where the rains are just enough in a good year and nothing like enough in a bad one, and where the black soil that holds water so well in the wet years bakes and cracks in the dry ones.

The other collection’s famines all fell in this belt. The famine of 1630–32 emptied Khandesh and the Ahmadnagar country; the Doji Bara of 1791–92, which Richard Grove has tied to the great El Niño of those years, took the Deccan and the Circars; and the famine of 1876–78, which lies just outside the timeline’s frame, killed something over five million people in the Bombay and Madras Deccan, Mysore and Hyderabad, worst of all in Bellary and its neighbours – the very districts Munro had settled with the ryot eighty years before. The Famine Commission of 1880, which sat after it, drew the ‘famine tract’ of the peninsula on a map, and the tract is the rain shadow, almost line for line. What the Commission proposed – famine codes, relief works, the railways as a means of moving grain – was the first systematic attempt to administer the shadow rather than suffer it.

The shadow is not fixed. Its edge moves with the strength of each monsoon, and the plateau’s drought years cluster with the failures of the Indian Ocean’s larger weather; the monsoon assembled in the Cenozoic still delivers its water on the escarpment’s terms. What the rock did was to fix where the risk would lie – on the drier, poorer, cash-assessed ground east of the crest – and what the states did, one after another, was to tax that ground as if the good years were the rule. The famine tract and the audit belt of the other collection are the same country.

In the story

The escarpment decided who would be hungry. Every famine in the Deccan timeline, and the Commission that finally mapped them, is an entry about this shadow – the one place where the plateau’s geology reached most directly into its politics, and did so through the weather.

entry.title: New entry: The rift coast and the ports
entry.summary: The west coast is a rift scar: a straight edge torn when the Seychelles left, with a narrow shelf below the escarpment and few harbours in it. Where the sea drowned a river mouth there was a port, and the ports – Goa, Chaul, Dabhol, Bhatkal, and at last Bombay – were the doors through which every outside power came.
entry.content:
The coast that runs from Surat to Cape Comorin was made twice. The southern stretch, the Malabar and Kanara coast, is the edge Madagascar left about 88 million years ago; the northern, the Konkan, is the younger tear of the Seychelles rifting around 65 million years ago, cut through the still-warm Traps, with the Panvel flexure near Bombay tilting the lava flows down toward the sea. A rifted margin has a characteristic shape and the Konkan has it: a coastline drawn almost straight for six hundred kilometres, a coastal plain thirty to sixty kilometres wide of laterite-capped tablelands and rice valleys, and behind it the escarpment, the rift’s uplifted shoulder. Such a coast offers little to a ship. It has no bays worth the name; the rivers that reach it are short and steep, and their mouths, drowned by the sea’s rise since the last ice age, make creeks – estuaries with a bar across the entrance and a tidal channel behind – rather than harbours.

The creeks were the ports. Sopara and Kalyan in antiquity, Thana, Chaul, Dabhol, Rajapur and Vengurla in the sultanate centuries, Goa on the Mandovi and Zuari, Karwar, Bhatkal and Honavar on the Kanara coast: each was a river mouth where a ship could lie inside the bar and a road climbed to a pass. The horse trade of the Deccan timeline came in through them, which is why Bijapur and Vijayanagara fought over Goa and why Albuquerque wanted it; the Portuguese layer of the Deccan was a chain of creek forts, and the Marathas’ sea power under Kanhoji Angre rested on the same geography – Kolaba, Suvarnadurg and Vijaydurg on rocky headlands and islets commanding the creeks, Sindhudurg on a rocky islet off Malvan. One place was different. At Bombay a cluster of basalt islands and a drowned valley behind them made the one deep, sheltered anchorage on the whole Konkan coast, and the Company, which had held a creek factory at Surat for half a century, understood what that meant when it took the islands from the Crown in 1668. Bombay became the port of the Deccan because the rift had made a harbour there and nowhere else.

The coast still sorts its history by geology. The laterite tablelands carry the Konkan’s villages and its old forts; the creeks carry its fishing towns; and the one harbour carries the city that, in the other collection, turned the plateau’s cotton into a boom and its debts into a riot.

In the story

The rift decided where the sea could reach the land, and so where the outsiders came ashore: a straight coast with a dozen creeks and a single harbour. The Portuguese, the Angres and the Company are, in this reading, three ways of holding the same few doors.

entry.title: New entry: Black soil and the bonds
entry.summary: The Traps weather into a black clay that holds water and grows cotton; the survey put a price on it, the American war put a market under it, and the debt that followed the market is what the Riots Commission found in the moneylenders’ bonds.
entry.content:
The Deccan’s history in the last period of this collection was written on one soil. Where the Traps have weathered in a dry climate they leave regur – the black cotton soil of the companion collection – a deep, cracking clay that swells in the rains, holds moisture through the dry months and will carry a crop with no more water than falls on it. It floors Khandesh, Berar, the Nagpur country, Marathwada and the southern Maratha districts from Sholapur to Bijapur, and it spills south onto the limestones of the Bhima. It is the soil of cotton, and cotton is why the plateau’s villages had a cash crop before they had a cash economy.

The Company measured it first. The revenue survey that Goldsmid and Wingate began in 1835 and codified in the Joint Report of 1847 was, before it was anything else, a survey of soil: every field was measured and its soil classed by colour and depth, black above red above the thin ‘barad’ of the uplands, and the assessment was fixed on the class for thirty years. The old regimes had taxed a village’s share of the harvest; the new one taxed a field’s share of the geology, in cash, on a date. Then the American Civil War closed the Lancashire mills’ supply in 1861 and Bombay’s buyers came up the ghats for whatever the black soil would grow. Berar, assigned to the Company in 1853 and reached by rail in the same decade, became the cotton province of India; the Deccan’s older varieties and the American seed that Dharwar had grown since the 1840s went out through Bombay at prices no one had seen. Land was ploughed that had never been, credit followed the price into every taluka, and for four years the regur was the most valuable ground in the peninsula.

The tide went out in 1865. Prices fell by half; the thirty-year settlements of the 1830s came up for revision in the same years, and the revised assessments of Indapur and its neighbours were raised; the seasons of the early 1870s were poor. The debts contracted in the boom had been secured, under the new courts, on the land itself, and the moneylender who had lent against a cotton price now held bonds against fields. The Riots of May and June 1875 broke out not in the deep black soil of Berar but on its thin margin – Bhimthadi, Indapur, Supa, Parner, the talukas of Poona and Ahmednagar where the regur gives way to lighter ground and a cash assessment on a fixed date is hardest to meet. The cultivators burned the bonds, not the moneylenders; they wanted the paper.

What the Commission of 1876 described, without quite saying so, was a chain that ran from the rock to the register. The Traps made the soil; the soil grew the cotton; the survey classed the soil and fixed the demand; the war priced the cotton; the courts made the price into debt; and the debt, when the price fell, became the bonds in the moneylender’s house. Every link in it is an entry in one of this site’s two collections, and none of them explains the riots alone.

In the story

This is where the plateau’s two histories meet on one field. The audit of the last period – the survey, the Inam Commission, the Watan Act – was in the end a reckoning of the soil: who held which class of it, what it owed, and to whom. The Riots are the black soil answering.

entry.title: New entry: The doab from below
entry.summary: The wedge between the Krishna and the Tungabhadra is the oldest ground on the plateau, granite and gneiss with a gold belt through it; the two rivers that bound it were the only lines the rock offered, which is why two centuries of states fought over the wedge and none could hold it.
entry.content:
The Raichur doab is usually explained by its rivers. Explain it instead by what lies beneath, and the frontier becomes a fact of geology before it is a fact of politics. The doab sits on the Dharwar craton – the grey Peninsular Gneiss and the granites that welded it, with two Archaean greenstone belts threaded through it, one of which carries the gold of Hutti, worked in antiquity and mined today. Along its northern rim the gneiss dips under the limestones of the Bhima basin, and a few miles beyond, at Bijapur and Gulbarga, the Deccan Traps begin. The doab is therefore the place where the basalt country ends and the granite country starts: deep black soil on the basalt and the limestone to the north, black and red soils patched across the granite of the doab itself. Vijayanagara was a granite kingdom and the Bahmanis a basalt one, and the doab was the seam.

Granite country has no natural frontiers except its rivers. The plateau here is a low, open surface of boulder hills and thin, patchy soil, crossable in any direction, and the only lines that could not be argued with were the Krishna, running east along the trap edge, and the Tungabhadra, running north-east off the craton. Every state that reached the doab claimed to the far river and could hold only to the near one, because the wedge between had nothing to defend it but the two forts on its granite hills, Raichur and Mudgal, and the crossings at Raichur’s fords were what the forts were for. Maski, in the middle of the doab, carries the minor rock edict in which Ashoka is named by name – the earliest sovereign claim on the wedge, cut into the same granite – and Raichur’s fort walls carry inscriptions of the Kakatiyas who held it in 1294 and of the Vijayanagara kings and sultans who took it in turn. The doab was fought for from 1362 to 1520 and changed hands repeatedly without ever changing shape.

The rock also explains the doab’s value. It was not the richest land on either side – the black soil to the north and the irrigated valleys to the south were both better – but it was the crossing, and the crossing controlled the movement of horses, armies and grain between the two Deccans. When Talikota removed one of the two, the frontier vanished in a year: no one needed to hold a seam between two countries that had become one. The rivers went on flowing where they had, and in the twentieth century the Tungabhadra dam turned the granite wedge into the most irrigated ground in the region, which is the doab’s final joke on its history.

In the story

The doab is the collection’s clearest case of a frontier the ground supplied and the states merely occupied: two rivers on a granite floor, a seam between basalt and gneiss, and nothing between them worth more than the crossing.

entry.title: New entry: Charnockite and the Nilgiris
entry.summary: The dark, greasy-looking granulite named in 1893 from Job Charnock’s tombstone; the rock of the Nilgiris, the Shevaroys and the far south, where the craton’s floor was cooked deepest.
entry.content:
In 1893 Thomas Holland of the Geological Survey examined the stone of Job Charnock’s tomb in St John’s churchyard in Calcutta, cut two centuries earlier from the quarries of St Thomas Mount near Madras, and found under the microscope a rock that fitted none of the existing names: quartz and feldspar in a granitic fabric, with the pyroxene hypersthene where mica should have been. He called it charnockite, after the founder of the city the tombstone stood in, and in 1900 described the ‘charnockite series’ across the peninsula in a memoir that gave the word to petrology everywhere. It was a Deccan naming, like laterite’s: a European reading a rock in India and sending the name home.

Charnockite is a granulite – a rock metamorphosed at the base of thick continental crust, at 700 to 900 °C and depths of twenty to thirty kilometres, hot and dry enough that the water-bearing minerals broke down and pyroxene grew instead. Its dark, greenish, greasy look on a fresh surface comes from that history, and so does its distribution. South of a line through Bengaluru the Dharwar craton passes into the Southern Granulite Terrain, and the great massifs of the south are charnockite: the Nilgiris, a block of it lifted to 2,600 metres at Doddabetta; the Shevaroys and the Biligirirangans; the Palni and Cardamom hills beyond the Palghat gap. The Nilgiri rocks were cooked about 2,500 million years ago, in the same consolidation that made the Closepet Granite; the granulites of the far south, around Madurai and Trivandrum, were reworked again about 550 million years ago, when the pieces of Gondwana were being sutured and what is now Kerala was joined to Madagascar and East Africa.

The rock is where the collection’s basement meets its people. Charnockite from Pallavaram and St Thomas Mount built Madras, and the Mount is the hill from which the Deccan timeline’s Lambton measured his first baseline in 1802. The Nilgiris, the highest ground in the peninsula, are the one part of the plateau that stands above the level of the Traps: a block of the oldest crust over the youngest cover, cool enough for the Company to build a hill station on and for the tea that replaced the shola. The granulite hills, the Ghats and the gap at Palghat are also a boundary in the other timeline – the frontier of its southern conquests and its Mysore wars, and the edge of the country in which Vijayanagara’s nayakas became kings.

entry.title: New entry: Koyna and Killari
entry.summary: The stable plateau shook twice in living memory: at Koyna in 1967, where a new reservoir woke a fault in the Trap pile, and at Killari in 1993, where nothing had warned anyone – two earthquakes that rewrote what a craton is expected to do.
entry.content:
A craton is supposed to be quiet. The Indian shield sits far from any plate boundary, and until the 1960s the Trap country had no earthquake of note in the written record; the engineers who built on it assumed, reasonably, that the rock beneath them did not move. Two events undid the assumption. In the early hours of 11 December 1967 an earthquake of magnitude about 6.3 struck Koynanagar in the Sahyadri, a few kilometres from the Koyna dam, whose reservoir had been filling since 1962: about 180 people were killed, the township was wrecked, the dam cracked and held. Small shocks had begun as the water rose, and they have continued for decades in the pattern that has made Koyna the world’s type case of reservoir-triggered seismicity – the weight and the seepage of a filled reservoir, acting on faults already close to failure, bringing forward earthquakes the crust would otherwise have stored. The region has produced thousands of shocks since, several above magnitude 5, and a deep-drilling programme begun in the 2010s now watches the process from inside the rock.

Killari was worse and unexplained. At four in the morning of 30 September 1993 an earthquake of magnitude 6.2 struck the Latur and Osmanabad districts in the middle of the plateau, two hundred kilometres from the Ghats and far from any dam. The focus was shallow, in the Trap pile and the basement beneath it, and the villages of stone and mud on the black soil collapsed on their sleeping occupants: close to ten thousand people died in some fifty villages, one of the deadliest earthquakes ever recorded in a stable continental interior. No fault had been mapped there. The rupture reached the surface as a scarp about a kilometre long, and the argument since has been whether the earthquake reactivated an old structure in the basement or broke a new fault up through the flows. Either way the Deccan’s seismic map was redrawn: the zoning of the peninsula was revised and its lowest zone abolished, and the plateau’s villages are now built, in principle, to a code.

The two earthquakes are the plateau’s reminder that stability is a rate, not a state. The fractures of the Narmada–Son zone, the openings that carry the water between the flows, and the faults the Traps buried are all still there, loaded by the slow push of India into Asia. Koyna showed that a reservoir could trip one; Killari, that one could go off by itself.

entry.title: New entry: Chauth and sardeshmukhi
entry.summary: The quarter and the tenth: the Maratha claim to a fixed share of other sovereigns’ revenue, first levied by Shivaji, chartered by the emperor in 1719, and the legal form that shared sovereignty took in the eighteenth-century Deccan.
entry.content:
Chauth was a quarter. In the western Deccan of the seventeenth century the word already meant a share of the land revenue paid to a power that could otherwise ravage a district – the Portuguese of Daman paid it to the Koli chiefs of Ramnagar for the peace of their northern villages – and Shivaji made it a claim of state. From the 1660s his officers demanded a fourth of the assessed revenue of Mughal and Bijapuri districts that he did not govern, in Khandesh and the Surat country among others, in return for leaving them alone. The payment did not transfer the district, only a fraction of its income: a Mughal faujdar and a Maratha collector might work the same villages in the same season. Sardeshmukhi was a further tenth, claimed on a different ground. The sardeshmukh was the chief of the hereditary district headmen, and Shivaji asserted the office over the whole of his swarajya as a right older than any sultan or emperor, which none of them had conferred and none could withdraw.

The two claims paid for the long war after 1689. Rajaram at Jinji and Tarabai after him could not maintain an army from a territory they did not hold, so they granted their commanders the right to collect chauth and sardeshmukhi from Mughal districts, as saranjam, and the commanders collected what they could; the Maratha polity that emerged after 1707 was in large part a federation of such grants. The sanads of 1719 then gave the arrangement an imperial seal. The emperor granted Shahu the chauth and sardeshmukhi of the six Mughal subahs of the Deccan – Khandesh, Berar, Aurangabad, Bidar, Bijapur and Hyderabad – and the Marathas undertook to keep the peace they were being paid for. Under the Peshwa’s rules the chauth was itself divided: a quarter of it, the babti, went to the Chhatrapati; a small share, the sahotra, to the Pant Sachiv; and the bulk, the mokasa, to the commanders who collected it and kept horse on it. Sardeshmukhi went to the king.

What this meant for sovereignty is the subject of André Wink’s Land and Sovereignty in India. On his reading the Maratha claim was not a tribute exacted from a defeated empire but a share in it – a co-sovereignty negotiated district by district, in which the Mughal governor kept his office and the Maratha kamavisdar kept his fourth, and each recognised the other as the condition of collecting anything at all. The Nizam’s Hyderabad after 1724 lived under exactly this partition, enforced at Palkhed and contested to Kharda; so did Malwa and Gujarat once the Peshwa carried the claim north of the Narmada. The Company inherited the claim in 1818 with the Peshwa’s other rights and let it lapse, because a paramount power collects revenue and does not share it.

In the story

Chauth is the mechanism behind the collection’s argument: the fraction that let two states hold one territory and one taxpayer with a legal title each. Most of the entries from Palkhed to the Peshwa’s surrender are, underneath, about who held it.

entry.title: New entry: The Gajapatis of Orissa
entry.summary: The Suryavamsi kings of Orissa – Kapilendra, Purushottama, Prataparudra – pushed down the Andhra coast for eighty years and were the third power of the Deccan’s first two periods, until Krishnadevaraya drove them back to the Krishna.
entry.content:
Kapilendra Deva took the throne of Orissa in 1434–35 at the end of the Eastern Ganga line and gave his house the title Gajapati, lord of elephants. In the scheme the inscriptions of the age use, that was one of three sovereignties in the subcontinent, beside the Narapati, lord of men, which Vijayanagara claimed, and the Ashvapati, lord of horses, which was the sultans’ share; the title was a programme, and for a generation the Gajapatis acted on it. Kapilendra’s armies came down the coast through the Reddi and Velama country, took Rajahmundry and Kondavidu in the 1450s, intervened in the Bahmani succession, and by the 1460s were raiding far to the south. Oriya tradition and the inscriptions claim Kanchi and a tribute from the Tamil country, and Vijayanagara under Mallikarjuna could not stop them.

Purushottama (1467–97) held the Andhra conquests and lost the far south. His son Prataparudra (1497–1540) inherited a frontier on the Krishna that Vijayanagara now meant to move, and Krishnadevaraya’s eastern war of 1513–19 was the longest campaign of his reign. Udayagiri, the hill fort at the southern end of the Gajapati domain, fell in 1514 after a siege of more than a year; Kondavidu in 1515, with a Gajapati prince among the prisoners; then Kondapalli, Rajahmundry and Simhachalam, where the king had his victory recorded on the temple walls, and a march to the Gajapati capital at Cuttack. The peace of 1519 gave Vijayanagara everything south of the Krishna and gave Krishnadevaraya a Gajapati princess as a queen. The river became the frontier between the two Hindu kingdoms and, within a few years, the line along which Golconda advanced instead.

The Gajapatis did not long survive the settlement. Prataparudra’s successors were murdered in turn, a minister’s family took the throne in 1541, and the Qutb Shahs, then the Mughals, absorbed the coast the dynasty had ruled; Kondavidu and Kondapalli, which had passed from Reddi to Gajapati to Raya within a lifetime, were Golconda’s by the middle of the century.

The Gajapati century matters here because it breaks the symmetry of ‘two Deccans’. For eighty years there were three sovereignties on the plateau’s eastern edge, and the third was Hindu, claimed the same imperial titles as Vijayanagara, and fought it as readily as it fought the sultans. The coalition politics of the 1560s were rehearsed on the Krishna frontier a generation earlier, with Orissa in the third seat.

entry.title: New entry: Munro and the Ceded Districts
entry.summary: The districts the Nizam surrendered to the Company in 1800 as the price of its protection, and the collector who settled them field by field with the cultivator himself: the ryotwari system that Madras adopted and that Bombay argued with for fifty years.
entry.content:
By the treaty of 12 October 1800 the Nizam gave up to the Company the territory he had received in the partitions of Mysore in 1792 and 1799 – the country between the Tungabhadra and the Penner that became the Ceded Districts of Bellary and Cuddapah – in return for an enlarged subsidiary force he would no longer have to pay for. It was a raw acquisition: poligar chiefs in their forts, a revenue system disordered by Haidar, Tipu and the Nizam’s farmers in turn, and no Company officer who had governed there. Thomas Munro, a Scottish officer who had spent seven years under Alexander Read settling the Baramahal after 1792, arrived in October 1800 as principal collector, with four assistants and a country of about 27,000 square miles. He reduced the poligars in his first two years, some by pension and several by force, and then did what he had begun to do in the Baramahal: he settled the revenue with each cultivator directly, on a field-by-field survey and assessment, with no intermediary between the ryot and the state.

Ryotwari, as the system came to be called, was a theory of Indian society as much as a method of collection. Munro held that the village and its headman were the ancient institutions of the country, that the zamindars of Bengal and the revenue farmers of the sultanates were parasites upon them, and that the state should deal with the peasant proprietor, assess him moderately and for a fixed term, and leave the village to run itself. His reports from the Ceded Districts, written in the plain and confident prose that made him the most quoted of Company administrators, went to Madras and to London and into the Fifth Report of 1812. Madras adopted the system for the whole presidency in the 1820s, when Munro returned as governor; he died of cholera on tour at Pattikonda, in the Ceded Districts, in July 1827.

Bombay took the argument and not the method. Elphinstone read Munro’s reports and shared his respect for the village, but the Deccan the Company took in 1818 was full of hereditary rights – watans, inams, saranjams – for which Munro’s theory had no place. The survey that Pringle began in the 1820s tried to apply a Ricardian version of the ryotwari assessment and failed; the settlement Goldsmid and Wingate made from 1835 was ryotwari in principle and something more complicated in practice. The Ceded Districts are where the paramount power first tried to reach past every intermediate layer to the man who held the plough; the Bombay Deccan is where it discovered how many layers there were.

entry.title: New entry: The murder of Narayanrao and Ramshastri’s verdict
entry.summary: The killing of the Peshwa in his own palace on 30 August 1773, the judge who found his uncle responsible, and the council of ministers that ruled for twenty years in the name of a child born after his father’s death.
entry.content:
Narayanrao was seventeen when he became Peshwa in November 1772 on the death of his brother Madhavrao, and he held the office for nine months. His uncle Raghunathrao, who had expected the succession and had already been confined once for intriguing against Madhavrao, was under house arrest in the Shaniwar Wada; the Gardis, the Peshwa’s own regiment of matchlockmen under Sumer Singh, had a grievance over pay and a grudge over their treatment. On 30 August 1773, during the Ganesh festival, a party of Gardis broke into the palace and killed the Peshwa and several of those who tried to shelter him. The tradition that Raghunathrao’s written order to seize his nephew – dharave – was altered by his wife Anandibai to marave, kill him, is old and cannot be proved; the order to seize is not doubted.

Raghunathrao took the seals. What followed was unusual in any state of the age. Ramshastri Prabhune, the nyayadhish or chief judge of the Peshwa’s court, examined the killing, named Raghunathrao as responsible, and pronounced that no penance short of giving up the office could expiate it; he then left Pune rather than serve the man he had condemned. The verdict had no army behind it and could not be executed, but it gave the opposition its ground. Over the following months the leading ministers and sardars – Sakharam Bapu Bokil, Nana Phadnavis, Trimbakrao Pethe, with Holkar and Scindia – formed the council that Maratha historians call the Barbhai, the twelve brethren, in the name of Narayanrao’s widow Gangabai and the child she was carrying. Sawai Madhavrao was born at Purandar fort on 18 April 1774 and invested as Peshwa at forty days old. Raghunathrao, beaten in the field, fled to the Company at Surat and signed away Salsette and Bassein for its support: the war that ended at Wadgaon and Salbai begins here, and so does the regency that governed Pune until 1795.

The episode is a sovereignty judged from within. A state whose power ran through the Chhatrapati’s minister had, in Ramshastri, an officer whose authority came from the dharma he administered rather than the office he served, and who could say that a Peshwa had forfeited the right to be one. The council that acted on his finding ruled for a generation without a Peshwa of age; and the Company, which had backed the loser, learned that Maratha sovereignty was not to be captured by capturing a claimant.

entry.title: New entry: Nagpur, from Raghuji to the lapse
entry.summary: The fourth Maratha house, which ruled Berar and the Gond country from Nagpur for a century, raided Bengal, fought the Company at Sitabaldi, and ended in December 1853 as the largest of the states taken by lapse.
entry.content:
Raghuji Bhonsle, a kinsman of the Chhatrapati’s family whom Shahu made Senasahibsubha in 1728, took Nagpur from the Gond raja of Deogarh in the 1740s and made it the capital of a state that ran from Berar across the Gondwana forests to Orissa. His horsemen raided Bengal from 1742 until Alivardi Khan bought them off in 1751 with Orissa and the chauth of Bengal. The house was one of the four great sardar families of the confederacy, but the one that stayed a Deccan power, on the plateau’s north-eastern edge between Hyderabad and the Ganges plain. Raghuji died in 1755; his sons quarrelled; and Nagpur settled into the shape it kept for sixty years, a Maratha court ruling a country that was largely Gond, Telugu and Oriya, with Berar’s cotton revenue as its treasury and the Nizam and the Peshwa as its rivals.

The house met the Company’s armies twice. In 1803 Raghuji II marched with Scindia and shared the defeats at Assaye and Argaon; the Treaty of Deogaon in December took Cuttack and the country west of the Wardha from him, and the Nizam received the Berar districts. In November 1817 his nephew and successor Appa Sahib, secretly in league with the Peshwa, attacked the Residency; the two-day battle on the Sitabaldi hills, held by a small force of Madras sepoys, was the eastern front of the Third Maratha War. Appa Sahib was deposed the next year, and the Company put a boy, Raghuji III, on the gadi under a Resident, Richard Jenkins, who governed in his name until 1830 and then handed him a state whose army and foreign relations were already the Company’s.

Raghuji III died on 11 December 1853 without a son and without having adopted one. His widows proposed an adoption; Dalhousie declined to recognise one made after the raja’s death and declared the state lapsed to the paramount power, on the doctrine that had taken Satara five years earlier. Nagpur became a Company province in 1854 and, joined to the Saugor and Nerbudda territories, the Central Provinces in 1861; the raja’s jewels, horses and elephants were sold at auction, which was remembered. Of the four houses of the confederacy Nagpur was the only one to disappear. Holkar, Scindia and the Gaekwad survived 1858 as princes because they had heirs, treaties and, in 1857, the sense to stay loyal.

entry.title: New entry: Sringeri, 1791
entry.summary: In April 1791 Maratha irregulars sacked the Sringeri matha; the Swami turned to Tipu Sultan, whose letters ordering its restoration, found in 1916, are the best-documented act of his religious policy.
entry.content:
Sringeri, on the Tunga in the Malnad, was the oldest of the mathas that trace themselves to Shankara, and its Jagadguru was the most eminent Hindu prelate in Mysore. In April 1791, in the second year of the Third Anglo-Mysore War, the Maratha army under Parashuram Bhau Patwardhan was moving through the Malnad as the Company’s ally, and a body of the irregulars attached to it – pindaris and Lamanis, the camp’s unpaid followers, with a Patwardhan detachment under Raghunath Rao of Kurundwad – fell on the matha. They plundered its treasury and granaries, killed a number of Brahmins and others, carried off an elephant and the ornaments of the shrine, and threw down the image of Sharada. The Swami, Sacchidananda Bharati, fled. The Marathas’ own letters, printed by Khare, record the Peshwa’s displeasure and Nana Phadnavis’s orders for restitution, which followed slowly and in part.

The Swami wrote to Tipu. Some thirty of Tipu’s replies, in Kannada, with the orders they carried to his officers, were found in the matha’s records and published by the Mysore Archaeological Department in 1916. They express the sultan’s outrage in the language of dharma – people who had sinned against so holy a place were sure to suffer for it in this Kali age – direct the Asaf of Bednur to supply money and grain for the re-consecration of the image, ask the Swami to perform rites for the prosperity of the state, and continue in the same tone of respect to the end of the reign. Earlier grants by Haidar and Tipu to the matha are on record, and so are Tipu’s gifts to the temples of Srirangapatna, Melkote and Nanjangud.

What the letters prove is narrower than either side of the modern argument wants. They do not cancel the deportations from Coorg and Malabar, or the destruction recorded in Company and Nair accounts; they show a ruler at war treating the great institution of his Hindu subjects as a source of legitimacy and of prayer for victory – kingship as an idiom to be mastered, as Brittlebank reads it, rather than a creed to be imposed, of a piece with his regulations and his embassies. The raid, for its part, was the work of the Deccan’s plural military market: the army that sacked Sringeri was the ally of the Company that would storm Srirangapatna, and its irregulars answered to no one.
